passage: During the Tuesday spelling test, Usha saw Imran slide a folded paper out of his pencil box and peek at it. After that, nothing he did looked right to her. When the art teacher pinned Imran's drawing of a heron on the class board, Usha whispered to her bench partner, "He probably traced it." At lunch Imran offered her half his orange. She shook her head. "He only shares so people will like him," she told Deepa later. When Imran helped a younger boy pick up spilled crayons in the corridor, Usha rolled her eyes and walked faster. The heron stayed on the board all week, its grey feathers carefully shaded, and Usha never once looked at it.

qa.q: What did Usha see Imran do during the spelling test?
qa.a: She saw Imran slide a folded paper out of his pencil box and peek at it.

qa.q: Why does it feel reasonable to Usha to doubt Imran's drawing and his kindness?
qa.a: Having seen him cheat once, Usha feels she now knows who he really is, so every good act looks like a trick to her.

qa.q: What could Usha try the next time she thinks badly of Imran?
qa.a: She could ask herself whether she would doubt the heron drawing if she had never seen the test, and judge each thing on its own.

qa.q: What is it like for Imran when Usha keeps turning away from him?
qa.a: Imran keeps being friendly and gets cold looks back, so he may feel shut out without knowing why his orange and his drawing count for nothing.

grounding: A girl who saw a classmate cheat once lets it spoil her view of his drawing and his friendliness.

passage: I'm Joel, Sudha's older brother, and I walk her home from school. Last month she came out furious: a boy called Tanvir had copied answers from the girl beside him during the maths test. Fair enough to be upset. But since then, everything about Tanvir is wrong. His kite at the colony ground? "Ugly colours." When he waved at her from his cycle, she said he was "being fake." Yesterday his team won the quiz and she muttered that he must have cheated again, though quiz answers are shouted out loud. I can't see inside her head. Maybe she's still hurt about the test, maybe something else happened. I just know Tanvir waved again today, and she looked at the ground.

qa.q: What did Tanvir do during the maths test?
qa.a: Tanvir copied answers from the girl beside him during the maths test.

qa.q: Why might Sudha feel sure that Tanvir cheated in the quiz too?
qa.a: Once she saw him copy, Sudha may feel she has found out what kind of boy he is, so even a quiz win looks like another trick to her.

qa.q: How could Joel gently help Sudha see Tanvir more fairly?
qa.a: Joel could ask her to name one thing Tanvir did that had nothing to do with the test, like the kite or the quiz, and let her think about it.

qa.q: How might Tanvir read Sudha's reaction to his waving?
qa.a: Tanvir might be puzzled or hurt when a friendly wave gets a stare at the ground, since he may not even know she saw the test.

grounding: An older brother watches his sister let one cheating incident spoil her view of a boy's kite, friendliness and quiz win.

passage:
Monday. In the class test, Avni saw Jomon turn his paper so he could read Ritu's answers. She said nothing, but her stomach went tight.
Wednesday. Jomon brought his model of a lighthouse for the science fair, with a tiny bulb that really blinked. Everyone crowded round. Avni stood back. "Someone else made it for him," she said, though nobody had asked. When he offered to help fix her loose wire, she said she didn't need help from a cheat.
The next Friday. Miss Joseph asked Jomon to show the class how he wired the bulb. He explained each step, stumbling a little, drawing it on the board. Avni watched his careful sketch and felt unsure. Maybe he had made it himself after all.

qa.q: What did Jomon bring to the science fair?
qa.a: Jomon brought his model of a lighthouse, with a tiny bulb that really blinked.

qa.q: How can you tell the test was still shaping what Avni thought of Jomon?
qa.a: She decided someone else made his model and called him a cheat when he offered help, because the test was the lens she saw him through.

qa.q: What small step could help Avni judge the lighthouse fairly?
qa.a: She could ask Jomon how he built it, the way Miss Joseph did, before deciding it wasn't his work.

qa.q: What might Jomon feel when Avni refuses his help with the wire?
qa.a: Jomon may feel stung or confused, since he offered something kind and was called a cheat for it.

grounding: Across three days, a girl lets one act of copying make her doubt a boy's model and his kindness, then begins to waver.

passage: The lights went out in the middle of the chemistry practical, and the lab fell into grey afternoon gloom. Jomon kept working by the window, counting drops carefully, and finished his titration first. His readings were neat, three trials within a whisker of each other. Mr Pillai walked past without looking at the sheet. Two minutes later Jomon knocked a stool with his foot. "Of course. Jomon again," Mr Pillai said. "Our naughty champion since Class 8." A few students laughed. Avni, at the next bench, leaned over. "Your numbers are better than mine," she whispered. Jomon shrugged and turned the sheet face down. On the bus home he didn't open his notebook at all. What was the point of trying, he thought, if only the stool got noticed?

qa.q: What did Mr Pillai say when Jomon knocked a stool?
qa.a: Mr Pillai said, 'Of course. Jomon again,' and called him 'our naughty champion since Class 8.'

qa.q: What is Jomon thinking on the bus home?
qa.a: He wonders what the point of trying is if only the stool gets noticed, so he feels his careful work doesn't count. 😔

qa.q: How could Mr Pillai handle the next practical better?
qa.a: He could look at every sheet before commenting and name Jomon's neat readings as clearly as he names his slips.

qa.q: How does Avni see Jomon's work compared with the teacher?
qa.a: Avni actually looks at his sheet and sees his numbers are better than hers, while Mr Pillai only noticed the stool.

grounding: A teacher's old 'naughty' label means a boy's careful practical goes unseen while one clumsy slip is called out.

passage: Amandeep had rewritten his Hindi essay twice, once at the dining table and once on the balcony of their Pune flat while the pressure cooker whistled. He handed it in on Monday, a day early. On Thursday the essays came back. Mrs Rao read three aloud and praised their opening lines. Amandeep's had a big tick and nothing else. Then, when his phone buzzed in his bag during the last period, she stopped the class. "Some people never change," she said, looking straight at him. "Trouble from day one." Chandrika turned around and mouthed, "Yours was good, I read it." Amandeep nodded, but his ears were hot. At home he pushed the essay into the back of a drawer without showing anyone.

qa.q: When did Amandeep hand in his Hindi essay?
qa.a: He handed it in on Monday, a day early.

qa.q: What do Amandeep's hot ears and hidden essay suggest he feels?
qa.a: They suggest he feels embarrassed and unseen, since his careful essay got only a tick while one buzzing phone drew a public comment.

qa.q: What could Amandeep do so his effort gets seen?
qa.a: He could show the essay to someone at home, or ask Mrs Rao privately for feedback on it, so the work is looked at apart from the label.

qa.q: What would change if Mrs Rao read Amandeep's essay without her old picture of him?
qa.a: She might notice the rewriting, praise it like the others, and treat the buzzing phone as a small slip rather than proof.

grounding: A teacher who sees a boy as 'trouble' skips his careful essay but spotlights a single slip in front of the class.

passage:
"Why the long face, Dhruv?" Manoj bhaiya asked, dropping onto the sofa.
"Sir put my name on the board again. For talking."
"Were you talking?"
"I asked Farhan for a ruler. One word. Half the class chatted all period and nothing happened to them."
"And the maths test? You said you got nineteen out of twenty."
"He handed it back without a word. Last week, when I got twelve, he said, 'Lazy boys get lazy marks.'"
Manoj bhaiya was quiet for a moment. "So he only sees the twelve."
"He decided in Class 8 that I'm the lazy one. Nothing I do changes it."
"Your nineteen is real, even if he skipped it."
Dhruv picked at a loose thread on the sofa. "Then why does it feel like it doesn't count?"

qa.q: What mark did Dhruv get in the maths test?
qa.a: Dhruv got nineteen out of twenty.

qa.q: Why does Dhruv feel his good mark doesn't count?
qa.a: Sir handed back the nineteen in silence but called him lazy over a twelve, so Dhruv feels the label outweighs anything he does.

qa.q: What small step could Manoj suggest to help Dhruv?
qa.a: He could suggest Dhruv keep his marked work together and ask a parent or trusted teacher to raise the pattern calmly with Sir.

qa.q: How does Manoj bhaiya see the situation?
qa.a: Manoj bhaiya sees that the teacher only notices the twelve, and he reminds Dhruv that the nineteen is real anyway.

grounding: A teenage boy explains how a teacher's 'lazy' label makes his good marks go unnoticed while small slips are punished.

passage: In the college library's discussion room, Uma had the project tracker open on her laptop. Four names, twelve tasks. "Ritvik gets nothing this time," she said. Jaya looked up. "Nothing? He's in the group." "He sent the literature review a day late in week two. I had to stay up formatting everything. I'm not risking the final report on him." "He had fever that week, remember?" "Still." Uma left his row empty and split his tasks between herself and Jaya. When Ritvik messaged offering to do the survey charts, she replied, "Covered, thanks." Later, alone in the room, she noticed that the charts he'd made for the midterm were the neatest in the whole file. She scrolled past them quickly.

qa.q: Why does Uma say Ritvik gets nothing this time?
qa.a: He sent the literature review a day late in week two, and she had to stay up formatting everything.

qa.q: Why does leaving Ritvik's row empty feel sensible to Uma?
qa.a: After losing sleep over his late part, Uma wants to protect the final report, so cutting him out feels like being careful rather than unfair.

qa.q: What could Uma do instead of scrolling past his charts?
qa.a: She could weigh his whole record, including the neat midterm charts and his fever, and give him the survey charts with a clear deadline.

qa.q: How might Jaya feel about suddenly carrying Ritvik's share?
qa.a: Jaya may feel uneasy, since she remembers he was ill and now has extra work because of a judgement she questioned.

grounding: A student lets one late submission define a groupmate and stops giving him work despite his neat charts.

passage:
Hi Minakshi,
Quick update from the hostel. Remember Aniket from my design project group? I've basically taken him off everything. He missed the first mock-up deadline by a whole day, and after that I just can't trust him. I've given his wireframes to Kavin and I'm doing the presentation slides myself.
Today he asked in the group chat if he could handle the user interviews. I said we'd already sorted it. Honestly it's easier this way. Although... Kavin told me Aniket's interview notes last semester were the best in the class, and that he'd been travelling home for a wedding that week. I don't know. I'm tired, and it's simpler not to depend on him.
Write soon,
Sharmila

qa.q: Who got Aniket's wireframes?
qa.a: Sharmila gave his wireframes to Kavin.

qa.q: What is Sharmila feeling when writing 'it's easier this way'?
qa.a: Sharmila sounds tired and wants to avoid another let-down, so leaning on nobody feels safer than giving Aniket a second chance.

qa.q: What would you advise Sharmila about the user interviews?
qa.a: Since Aniket's interview notes were the best in the class, Sharmila could give him that task with a check-in date instead of judging him by one late mock-up.

qa.q: How might Aniket experience being told everything is already sorted?
qa.a: Aniket may feel pushed out of his own project without knowing why, especially if he thinks the wedding trip explained the delay.

grounding: In an email, a student admits to writing off a groupmate after one late deadline and no longer giving him tasks.

passage: Okay, Sangeeta, you asked why Deven isn't doing anything in our marketing project. Honestly? Second week, he submitted the survey summary late. One day late. The professor marked the whole group down by two points. From that moment I decided he's just not dependable. I stopped assigning him anything and did his part myself. Now it's week nine, I'm exhausted, and he keeps saying, "Give me something, anything." My mother always says, "Lakshmi, you hold grudges like a bank holds gold." Maybe. But what if he's late again? I did check: he's been on time for every other assignment this term. It's just that one day keeps replaying in my head, louder than everything else.

qa.q: How many points did the professor take off for the late summary?
qa.a: The professor marked the whole group down by two points.

qa.q: What worry keeps Lakshmi from giving Deven any work?
qa.a: Lakshmi keeps thinking 'what if he's late again?', so that one day feels louder than all his on-time work. 😰

qa.q: What could Lakshmi try now, in week nine?
qa.a: Lakshmi could hand Deven one clear task with an early deadline and judge him on his whole term's record, not just week two.

qa.q: What is it like for Deven to keep asking for work?
qa.a: Deven is probably frustrated and embarrassed, shut out of his own project for one late day while he pleads, 'Give me something, anything.'

grounding: A student explains how one late submission made the speaker write off a groupmate and do all his work.

passage:
14 March
Long day. Jaya's invoice batch went out with the wrong tax code this morning and three clients called. By lunch I had half-written the email moving her off the billing team. Then I caught myself: I was picturing Jaya as careless, full stop, off one morning.
So I did what my first manager, Mrs Kulkarni, used to say: "Uma beti, check the file before you judge the face." I pulled the whole record. Fourteen months, forty-odd batches, one error before this. And the tax code changed last week; the update note went to everyone except her, because she was on leave.
Deleted the email. Tomorrow I'll sit with her, walk through the new code, and ask what would help.
Still annoyed about the calls, honestly. But annoyed isn't a verdict.
Uma

qa.q: What went wrong with Jaya's invoice batch?
qa.a: Jaya's invoice batch went out with the wrong tax code this morning and three clients called.

qa.q: What did Uma catch herself thinking at lunch?
qa.a: Uma noticed she was picturing Jaya as careless, full stop, off one morning, while still annoyed about the calls.

qa.q: Which choice worked for Uma, and why?
qa.a: Pulling the whole record worked, because it showed only one earlier error and a missed update note, and that changed her decision.

qa.q: How is Jaya affected by Uma's second look?
qa.a: Instead of losing her billing role over a note she never got, Jaya gets help learning the new code and keeps her place. 🙂

grounding: A team lead notices one error colouring her view and checks the person's full record and circumstances before deciding.

passage:
Urmila: Sumit's deck had last year's numbers on slide 6. Client noticed. 😠
Deepti: ouch. still dropping him from Friday's pitch?
Urmila: I was about to. Then I realised I'm only thinking about slide 6.
Urmila: pulled his last five decks. All clean. He built the whole hotel-chain pitch alone in Jan.
Deepti: true, that one was great
Urmila: also checked the shared folder. The finance sheet he used was labelled 'final' but it's the old one. Anyone could've grabbed it.
Deepti: so not a Sumit problem, a folder problem
Urmila: bit of both maybe. He should've cross-checked. I'll tell him that.
Urmila: but he stays on Friday. I'll ask him to own the numbers check this time 👍

qa.q: What was wrong on slide 6 of Sumit's deck?

qa.q: What did Urmila realise before dropping Sumit?
qa.a: Urmila realised she was only thinking about slide 6, so the anger from one mistake was shaping her whole view of him.

qa.q: Why is Urmila's plan for Friday a fair one?

qa.q: How does Deepti see the problem once the folder is checked?
qa.a: Deepti sees it as a folder problem more than a Sumit problem, since the wrongly labelled 'final' sheet could have fooled anyone.

grounding: A lead notices one slide error colouring her view and reviews a colleague's past work and the shared folder before deciding.

passage: At the milk collection centre in Kallur, Devika checked the morning register and frowned. Wasim had logged forty litres from the Patil farm as fourteen. The farmer had come shouting at seven. Her first thought was blunt: that boy is sloppy, move him to washing cans. She had the words ready. Then she stopped with the pen over the register. Was she deciding about Wasim, or about one angry morning? She flipped back through three months of his entries. Neat columns, correct totals, even a note where he'd caught her own mistake in April. Then she noticed the smudged carbon sheet he'd been using since the new books hadn't arrived. She called Wasim over, showed him the error, and asked him to read the totals aloud before signing, from today.

qa.q: How had Wasim logged the forty litres from the Patil farm?
qa.a: Wasim had logged forty litres from the Patil farm as fourteen.

qa.q: Why did moving Wasim to washing cans seem right to Devika at first?
qa.a: The farmer had come shouting at seven, so in that angry moment one error made Wasim look sloppy through and through.

qa.q: What countermeasure did Devika choose, and why does it help?
qa.a: She asked Wasim to read the totals aloud before signing, which guards against the real risk without punishing him for one slip.

qa.q: What would change for Wasim if Devika had acted on her first thought?
qa.a: He would have lost his register work despite three months of neat entries and even catching her own mistake in April.

grounding: A supervisor pauses on one register error, reviews the worker's full record and conditions, then decides.

passage: The lunch bell rang, and forty children poured into the narrow corridor outside Class 4B. Advait was squeezed against the wall when Gopika's elbow hit his shoulder and his water bottle clattered to the floor. "She did that on purpose," he told Sangeeta Ma'am, rubbing his arm. "She's always like that." Ten minutes later, racing back for his forgotten tiffin, Advait crashed straight into a Class 2 boy, who stumbled. "It wasn't my fault," Advait said quickly. "It's too crowded, and I was in a hurry." Sangeeta Ma'am raised an eyebrow. "So when you bump someone, it's the corridor. When Gopika bumps you, it's Gopika?" Advait opened his mouth, then closed it.

qa.q: What happened to Advait's water bottle?
qa.a: His water bottle clattered to the floor when Gopika's elbow hit his shoulder.

qa.q: Why does it feel true to Advait that Gopika did it on purpose?
qa.a: His arm hurts and he only feels the bump, not the forty children pushing Gopika, so meanness seems the obvious reason.

qa.q: What could Advait ask himself the next time someone bumps him?
qa.a: He could ask, 'Was it crowded, like when I bumped the Class 2 boy?' before deciding the person meant it.

qa.q: How might the Class 2 boy see Advait's excuse?
qa.a: The Class 2 boy only felt himself stumble, so he might think Advait was rough, just as Advait thought about Gopika.

grounding: A boy blames a classmate's nature for a bump in a packed corridor but blames the crowd when he bumps someone himself.

passage: I'm Vandana, Nakul's didi, and I ride the school bus with him. Yesterday the bus braked hard near the flyover and Madhuri, from his class, fell against him. His juice box squashed all over his shorts. "Madhuri is so rude," he announced to the whole back row. "She pushes everyone." I didn't see her push anyone; half the bus lurched forward. This morning, the same thing: brakes, lurch, and Nakul fell onto a Class 6 boy's lap. "The driver did it!" he said, laughing. I can't know what he was really thinking. But I noticed that when he fell, it was the bus, and when Madhuri fell, it was Madhuri.

qa.q: Where did the bus brake hard yesterday?
qa.a: The bus braked hard near the flyover.

qa.q: Why might Nakul feel so sure that Madhuri is rude?
qa.a: His juice squashed all over his shorts, so it may have felt personal to him, even though half the bus lurched.

qa.q: How could Vandana help Nakul see both falls the same way?
qa.a: Vandana could remind him of his own fall this morning and ask whether Madhuri might have been thrown by the brakes too.

qa.q: What is it like for Madhuri to be called rude in front of the back row?
qa.a: Madhuri may feel embarrassed and unfairly blamed for something the brakes caused.

grounding: An older sister notices her brother blaming a classmate's character for a bus bump while blaming the driver for his own.

passage:
Tuesday. In the crowded line for the drinking tap, Hafsa jostled Nitin and his shirt got soaked. "You did that on purpose," he snapped. At home he told Mummy that Hafsa was the meanest girl in Class 5.
Thursday. Nitin was carrying chart paper up the packed stairwell after assembly and knocked Hafsa's glasses clean off her face. "Sorry! The stairs were full," he said, and felt that was completely fair.
The next Monday. Miss Grace asked the class to draw the tap line as a bird would see it. Nitin drew thirty tiny heads squeezed together, with one small figure at the front being pushed. He looked at his drawing for a long time, then quietly said to Hafsa, "Maybe the line pushed you too."

qa.q: What did Nitin knock off Hafsa's face on Thursday?
qa.a: He knocked Hafsa's glasses clean off her face.

qa.q: Why did Nitin feel his own bump on the stairs was completely fair?
qa.a: He knew the stairs were full and his arms were full of chart paper, so his own reasons were clear to him in a way Hafsa's weren't.

qa.q: Which step helped Nitin see the tap line differently?
qa.a: Drawing the line from above showed thirty heads squeezed together, so the crowd became visible, not just Hafsa.

qa.q: How might Hafsa feel when Nitin says, 'Maybe the line pushed you too'?
qa.a: Hafsa may feel relieved that he finally sees it wasn't meanness, especially after he knocked her glasses off himself. 🙂

grounding: Over several days a boy blames a girl's character for a bump, excuses his own by the crowd, and slowly notices the situation.

passage: Hrithik, put the phone down for a minute. You've been saying Aman doesn't care since morning, just because he hasn't replied. Let your Tejas Chacha tell you something. When I was fifteen, my best friend Joseph and I were meant to go to the Dussehra mela together. I waited at the bus stand two hours. He never came. I was so sure he'd found cooler friends that I didn't speak to him for a month. Walked past him in the school corridor like he was a lamp post. Then his sister told me their father had been rushed to hospital that evening, and they had no phone at home. A month, beta. I lost a month with my best friend because I decided what kind of person he was. So charge your patience before you decide about Aman.

qa.q: How long did Tejas wait at the bus stand?
qa.a: Tejas waited at the bus stand two hours.

qa.q: Why was fifteen-year-old Tejas so sure Joseph didn't care?
qa.a: Waiting two hours alone hurt, and with no other information, 'he found cooler friends' felt like the only explanation.

qa.q: What could Hrithik do before deciding Aman doesn't care?
qa.a: He could send one kind message asking if everything is okay, and keep in mind a dead phone or trouble at home.

qa.q: How might Joseph have felt when Tejas ignored him in the corridor?
qa.a: Joseph was coping with his father being rushed to hospital, so being treated like a lamp post by his best friend would have hurt even more.

grounding: An uncle recalls how, at fifteen, he blamed a friend's character for not turning up when a family emergency was the reason.

passage: Results were out at ten, and by noon Jahnavi had messaged Rafiq six times. "Got 91 in science!!" "Hello??" "Wow. Okay." No reply came. Rain hammered the tin roof of her tuition centre, and the power had gone twice. "He literally doesn't care," she told Pooja, stabbing her pen into the desk. "He replies to everyone else in two seconds. I'm just not important." She didn't wonder why the whole building's internet was down, or why Rafiq's mother had looked so worried at the market that morning. By evening she'd drafted a long, cold message ending the friendship. At eight, a call came from an unknown number. "Jahnavi? It's Rafiq. Phone fell in a puddle. Nani's in hospital. I saw your marks on Ammi's phone. Congratulations."

qa.q: How many times had Jahnavi messaged Rafiq by noon?
qa.a: By noon Jahnavi had messaged Rafiq six times.

qa.q: Why did 'He literally doesn't care' feel true to Jahnavi?
qa.a: She was excited about her 91 and he usually replies in two seconds, so his silence felt like a message about how little she mattered.

qa.q: What could Jahnavi try before drafting a cold message?
qa.a: She could think of other reasons for the silence, like the rain, the power cuts or his worried mother, and wait to hear from him.

qa.q: What was Rafiq's day like while Jahnavi was angry?
qa.a: Rafiq had lost his phone in a puddle and his Nani was in hospital, yet he still called to congratulate her. 🙏

grounding: A teenager decides a friend doesn't care when he doesn't reply, ignoring clues of a dead phone and a family crisis.

passage: Gurleen's birthday cake sat half-eaten on the dining table of their Chandigarh flat, and she kept checking her phone. Wishes from cousins, from her tuition group, even from the aunty downstairs. Nothing from Nilesh, who lived two lanes away and had been her friend since Class 3. "Typical," she said to her mother. "He only remembers people when he needs notes." She scrolled back through old chats hunting for proof: the time he forgot to return her compass, the time he left early from her Holi party. Every memory seemed to fit. She did not think about his grandfather being unwell all month, or his phone screen being cracked for a week. At 11:40 pm, Nilesh knocked on the door, holding a crumpled card and a single laddoo.

qa.q: What was Nilesh holding when he knocked at 11:40 pm?
qa.a: Nilesh was holding a crumpled card and a single laddoo.

qa.q: Why did every old memory seem to fit for Gurleen?
qa.a: Once she decided Nilesh was selfish, she went hunting for proof, so the compass and the Holi party felt like evidence while his reasons stayed invisible.

qa.q: What would you advise Gurleen when a friend goes quiet on an important day?
qa.a: Pause before labelling him, remember what is happening in his life, like his unwell grandfather, and maybe ask if he's okay.

qa.q: What might it be like for Nilesh standing at the door that late?
qa.a: Nilesh may feel guilty for being so late and worried she's upset, even though he made the effort to come in person.

grounding: A teenager reads a friend's missing birthday wish as uncaring, overlooking his cracked phone and unwell grandfather.

passage:
"Vishal fell asleep in the lab again," Usha said, dropping a tray on the canteen table. "Third time this week."
"Maybe he's tired," said Paromita.
"Tired from what? Scrolling all night? He's just lazy. Our circuit report is due Friday and he's done one graph."
"Did you ask him?"
"Why should I? It's obvious."
Paromita stirred her tea. "He leaves the hostel at ten every night. I've seen him."
"Exactly. Partying."
"In a delivery jacket?"
Usha paused. "What?"
"A delivery company jacket. He comes back at five. His dad's shop shut last year, I think."
Usha looked down at the plate. "He never said anything."
"Would you, if everyone had already decided you were lazy?"

qa.q: What time does Vishal leave the hostel every night?
qa.a: He leaves the hostel at ten every night and comes back at five.

qa.q: Why does 'He's just lazy' feel obvious to Usha?
qa.a: Usha only sees Vishal asleep in the lab with one graph done; the night work is invisible, so a personal flaw seems the only cause.

qa.q: What could Usha do before Friday's report is due?
qa.a: Usha could talk to Vishal privately, ask what's going on, and plan the report around his hours.

qa.q: How does Paromita read Vishal's tiredness differently?
qa.a: Paromita has noticed the delivery jacket and his late returns, so she sees a hidden job and money pressure, not laziness.

grounding: A student calls a groupmate lazy for sleeping in the lab, not knowing he works night shifts.

passage: Last semester, in our supply chain group, I was the one who called Manoj lazy, loudly, in the group chat. He'd missed two meetings and his slides came in at 2 am, full of typos. I wrote, "Some of us actually care about grades." I'm Dhruv, and I've replayed that line a lot since. What I didn't know was that Manoj worked the night shift at a call centre near the station, eleven to six, to pay his sister's school fees. He saw my message and never argued back. I learned the truth from a senior who worked there too. Looking back, there were so many clues: the red eyes, the office lanyard in his bag, the way he always ate breakfast at noon. I just read every clue as proof of his character.

qa.q: What hours did Manoj work at the call centre?
qa.a: Manoj worked the night shift at a call centre near the station, eleven to six.

qa.q: How does Dhruv feel now about that line in the group chat?
qa.a: Dhruv seems regretful and a bit ashamed, having 'replayed that line a lot' since learning the truth. 😔

qa.q: What could Dhruv have done when the slides came in at 2 am?
qa.a: Dhruv could have messaged Manoj privately to ask whether something was going on, instead of posting a judgement in the group chat.

passage:
Mentor's note, Year 2 design project, Group C
During today's review, Suraj told me Wasim "does nothing and should get a lower grade." Wasim had missed both lab slots this week, and the prototype casing was unfinished. Suraj seemed genuinely angry, arms crossed, and said, "He just doesn't bother."
I spoke with Wasim separately. He has a night job at a bakery, to support his family, and had been nodding off at the lathe. He had not told the group, out of embarrassment.
With Wasim's permission, I told Suraj only that Wasim has a work commitment in the evenings. Suraj was quiet, then asked if the group could move its lab slot to mornings. We agreed on Tuesday and Thursday, 9 am.
Follow-up in two weeks.
Dr Rekha Menon

qa.q: Where does Wasim work at night?
qa.a: Wasim has a night job at a bakery, to support his family.

qa.q: What do Suraj's crossed arms and 'He just doesn't bother' suggest?
qa.a: They suggest Suraj felt genuinely angry and let down, reading the missed lab slots as proof that Wasim didn't care.

qa.q: How did Dr Menon support both students?
qa.a: Dr Menon spoke to Wasim privately, shared only what Wasim allowed, and helped the group move its lab slot to mornings.

qa.q: What is it like for Wasim to be called lazy while working nights?
qa.a: Wasim was already exhausted and embarrassed, so being told he doesn't bother likely added shame to a hard week.

grounding: A mentor records a student calling a groupmate lazy without knowing about his night job, and what changed once the pressure was known.

passage: I'm Salma, and I've shared a bay with Jatin for a year. On Monday, Ramesh from logistics shipped the wrong spare parts to the Nagpur warehouse, his second slip in a month. Half the floor was muttering that Ramesh is careless. Jatin didn't join in. He walked over to Ramesh's desk with two cups of tea and asked, "Rough few weeks? What's been going on?" I couldn't hear everything, but Ramesh talked a lot and kept pointing at his screen. Later Jatin told me the new stock system shows two parts with nearly identical codes. "Could be the system, could be Ramesh rushing. Maybe both," he said. By Friday he'd asked IT to flag similar codes, and asked Ramesh to double-check orders before lunch. I don't know what Jatin really thought. But nobody muttered on Friday.

qa.q: Where were the wrong spare parts shipped?
qa.a: Ramesh shipped the wrong spare parts to the Nagpur warehouse.

qa.q: What does Jatin's question 'Rough few weeks?' suggest about his thinking?
qa.a: It suggests Jatin was curious about what was happening for Ramesh rather than already sure he was careless. 🤔

qa.q: Why did Jatin's two-part fix make sense?
qa.a: Flagging similar codes deals with the system, and double-checking before lunch deals with any rushing, so both possible causes are covered.

qa.q: How might Ramesh have felt when Jatin came over with tea?
qa.a: While the floor muttered about him, Ramesh may have felt relieved that someone asked before judging, which is why he opened up.

grounding: A colleague watches another ask about a peer's situation before calling him careless, then address both system and habit.

passage:
Week one, Monday. Mohit's weekly sales report arrived at 3 pm instead of 10 am. Divyansh, his senior at the bank branch, felt the old irritation rising; "careless" was almost the word he typed in the reminder. He deleted it and wrote, "Everything okay? The report was late today."
Week one, Wednesday. They talked at the tea stall downstairs. Mohit said he'd moved to a flat across the city and the train now took ninety minutes. He also admitted, a bit sheepishly, that he'd always left reports to the last minute.
Week three, Monday. Divyansh had shifted Mohit's deadline to noon on Mondays, and Mohit had started drafting the report on Friday afternoons. It arrived at 11:20. Divyansh replied with one word: "Thanks."

qa.q: What time did Mohit's report arrive in week three?
qa.a: It arrived at 11:20.

qa.q: Why did Divyansh delete 'careless' from his reminder?
qa.a: He felt the irritation but wanted to know what was happening for Mohit before deciding, so he asked instead.

qa.q: What did Divyansh's solution get right?
qa.a: It dealt with both causes: the later deadline eased the long train ride, and drafting on Friday tackled Mohit's last-minute habit.

qa.q: How might Mohit have felt being asked 'Everything okay?' rather than scolded?
qa.a: Mohit probably felt safe enough to be honest, even admitting his last-minute habit a bit sheepishly.

grounding: Over three weeks a senior asks about a late colleague's circumstances before judging and finds both a long commute and a habit at play.

passage: Sit, Yusuf. You're ready to report Anil for leaving the ward keys again, I can tell. Let me tell you about Prakash. I was twenty-four, and Matron had just said, "Reena, you're in charge of nights now." Prakash kept forgetting to sign the medicine charts. Everyone said he was careless. I nearly wrote him up too. Instead, one night I asked him over chai, "What's happening on your shifts?" Turned out his nights clashed with his mother's hospital visits, and he was sleeping three hours. And yes, he also admitted he'd never liked paperwork. Both were true. We swapped his shifts, and I made him a small checklist to tick before handover. He became one of the best nurses I ever worked with. So before you decide who Anil is, ask what's going on. Then decide.

qa.q: What did Prakash keep forgetting to do?
qa.a: Prakash kept forgetting to sign the medicine charts.

qa.q: Why did young Reena ask Prakash over chai instead of writing him up?
qa.a: Reena was curious about what was happening on his shifts and didn't want to call him careless before knowing.

qa.q: What would Reena advise Yusuf to do about Anil?
qa.a: Ask Anil what's going on first and then decide, since a situation and a habit might both be true.

qa.q: How did Reena's approach change things for Prakash?
qa.a: Instead of being written up, Prakash got new shifts and a checklist, and he became one of the best nurses Reena worked with.

grounding: A senior nurse recalls asking about a colleague's circumstances before calling him careless and finding both a situation and a habit.

passage:
"We won!" Nilesh burst through the door, bat on his shoulder. "Thirty-two runs, didi! I hit the ball so perfectly, nobody could stop me."
"Nice!" said Gurleen, looking up from her homework. "And last Sunday?"
"Last Sunday doesn't count. The umpire was Pinku's cousin. Totally unfair."
"You were bowled first ball."
"Because the bat was cracked! Anyone would get out with that bat."
"Isn't that the same bat?"
Nilesh looked at the bat. "It's different today."
"How?"
"Today I was playing properly."
Gurleen grinned. "So when you win, it's you. When you lose, it's the umpire and the bat?"
"Obviously," said Nilesh, and went off to find a snack.

qa.q: How many runs did Nilesh score today?
qa.a: Nilesh scored thirty-two runs.

qa.q: Why does Nilesh insist last Sunday doesn't count?
qa.a: Losing feels bad, so blaming the umpire and the cracked bat lets Nilesh keep feeling like a great player.

qa.q: What question could help Nilesh learn from last Sunday?
qa.a: Someone could ask, 'If the bat and umpire were fine, what would you practise?' so he looks at his own play too.

qa.q: How does Gurleen see Nilesh's two stories?
qa.a: Gurleen notices it's the same bat both days and finds it funny that wins belong to him and losses to someone else. 😅

grounding: A boy credits his skill for a win but blames the umpire and his bat for a loss.

passage: I'm Jatin, and last week I played two carrom matches at our society's summer games. In the first one I beat Ramesh from C-wing. I told everyone it was because I have the best aim in the building. Mumma said, "Good boy, all that practice." In the second match I lost to Ramesh's little sister. I said the board was too dusty, the powder was bad and the striker was heavy. I even said she got lucky. Now when I think about it, the board and the striker were the same in both games. I think I only blamed them because losing to a Class 3 girl made my face hot.

qa.q: Where did Jatin play the two carrom matches?
qa.a: At the society's summer games.

qa.q: Why did Jatin blame the dust and the striker?
qa.a: Losing to a Class 3 girl made his face hot, so blaming the board felt better than admitting she played well.

qa.q: What could Jatin try after his next loss?
qa.a: He could name one thing the winner did well and one thing he could practise, before blaming the board.

qa.q: How might Ramesh's little sister feel hearing she just got lucky?
qa.a: She may feel her good play was brushed aside, when she really beat an older player on the same board.

grounding: A boy says he won through skill but blames the board, the striker and luck when he loses.

passage:
Coach's notes, Under-11 football, Saturday
Yusuf scored twice in the first half and ran to the sideline shouting, "Told you I'm the best striker!" In the second half we conceded three and lost. Yusuf said the referee was blind, the ball was flat and the goalkeeper was "useless." He kicked his water bottle.
After the match I asked him to list two reasons we won the first half. He said, "Me and... me." I laughed and asked who passed to him both times. He thought and said, "Shreyas." Then I asked for one thing he could have done better in the second half. That took longer. Eventually: "I stopped running back."
Plan: next week, each player names one thing a teammate did well.
Coach Reena

qa.q: How many goals did Yusuf score in the first half?
qa.a: Yusuf scored twice in the first half.

qa.q: Why was it easier for Yusuf to blame the referee and the ball?
qa.a: Losing stung his pride, and blaming the referee and the flat ball protected his feeling of being the best striker.

qa.q: How did Coach Reena help Yusuf see his own part?
qa.a: Coach Reena asked who passed to him and what he could have done better, so Yusuf named Shreyas and 'I stopped running back' himself.

qa.q: How might the goalkeeper feel about being called useless?
qa.a: The goalkeeper probably felt blamed and hurt for a loss the whole team shared. 😔

grounding: A coach notes a boy crediting himself for goals but blaming the referee, ball and keeper for the loss.

Maths: 94. Obviously. I've always had a brain for numbers, even Vikas said so when he saw my paper. I didn't revise the last chapter properly and still topped the section.
Chemistry: 58. The paper was ridiculous. Half the questions came from the tiny boxes at the side of the textbook, and Mrs Sen marks like she's angry at the world. Also I had a headache. Also the fan above my bench kept making that noise.
Vikas asked if I wanted to go through the chemistry paper with him and see what went wrong. I said no, there's nothing to learn from a badly set paper.
Now that I write it down, 'I didn't revise' is in the maths bit and not the chemistry bit. Weird. Whatever. Going to sleep.
Sunaina

passage: In the only photocopy shop on Bhadrachalam's market road, a crowd pressed around the printer as board results came out one by one. Yash's cousin Rashmi got her sheet first: 89 in social science. "I told you I'm naturally sharp," she announced to the shopkeeper, who hadn't asked. Then Yash's page slid out. Mathematics: 47. He folded it quickly. "The paper setter wanted us to fail," he said. "Question 14 wasn't even in the syllabus. And the invigilator kept walking up and down. How can anyone think?" Rashmi raised an eyebrow. "Question 14 was in the sample paper, Yash." "Sample paper is different," he muttered. On the tractor ride home he didn't take out the marks sheet once, and he didn't ask Rashmi how she'd studied.

qa.q: Which question did Yash say wasn't in the syllabus?
qa.a: Yash said Question 14 wasn't even in the syllabus.

qa.q: Why does Yash insist the sample paper is different?
qa.a: Admitting Question 14 was in the sample paper would mean he missed something, so blaming the setter protects how he sees himself.

qa.q: What could Yash do on the ride home that would actually help?
qa.a: He could look at the marks sheet and ask Rashmi how she studied, to find what to change next time.

qa.q: What would change if Rashmi had scored 47 and Yash 89?
qa.a: They would likely swap stories, with the low scorer blaming the paper and the high scorer claiming talent, since both are guarding their self-image.

grounding: One teen credits a high mark to natural sharpness while another blames a low mark on the setter and the invigilator.
